verdict: Caution on Jalna seed-plot and seed-processing borrowers: lend only to those with proven payment records and diversified crops, and avoid anyone tied to a single seed company or cotton alone.
title: Jalna Seeds: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
A Jalna seed borrower is usually a seed-plot grower or a small processor: it contracts farmers to multiply cotton, paddy or vegetable seed, buys the raw seed, conditions and packs it, and sells to a seed company or distributor. **Cash is made in one narrow window after harvest, and the whole model rests on the seed company paying on time.** The grower carries the field cost for a full season before any receipt; the processor carries inventory until the next sowing season. So when a proposal lands, check who the offtaker is and how long that offtaker has been paying; if the buyer is a single company, ask for its payment history with this borrower.

## Where value and cash sit
Value sits in the hybrid genetics and the quality of the seed lot, not in the field. **Pricing power belongs to the brand owner, not the grower, so margins are thin and fixed by the contract.** Working capital is the whole business: field advances out, seed inventory held, receivables from the seed company in. Capex is modest (conditioning, storage, testing). Peer results show the pattern: Kaveri's nine-month FY26 revenue was INR 1,221.56 crore, up 16.94% [4], yet Q4 FY26 carried a net loss of INR 25.65 crore amid inventory and cash-flow challenges [6]. A rating report notes the business is working-capital-intensive with high inventory and seasonality, with average utilisation at 66% of sanctioned limits from November 2024 to March 2026 [9]. So when a proposal lands, check inventory days and receivable days against the borrower's own prior year; if receivables are stretching while sales are flat, ask which buyer is delaying.

## What has broken now
Jalna is in drought, and the local report is blunt: Yashoda Seeds has not paid farmers for last year's seed-plot cotton, leaving growers stranded [2]. **That is a payment-chain break, not a weather story, and it is the single most important fact in this file.** Peer commentary confirms weak monsoon and lower demand hit revenue and profit, with margins held at 35% as cost of production fell [5]; Rallis reports inventory normalised and steady seed growth but flags input and freight cost pressure [7]. The rating sources are undated and should be treated as old [8][9][10][11]. Local coverage of Jalna itself is thin beyond the drought and payment report [1][2][3], so lean on first principles and peers here.

## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
**Pursue growers and processors contracted to more than one seed company, with vegetable, maize or paddy alongside cotton.** A rating report flags that 66% of one seed company's consolidated revenue came from cotton and paddy domestically [11] — concentration you should not mirror in your book. Avoid borrowers whose sole offtaker is a company with a reported payment delay [2], and avoid pure cotton-plot growers this season. Structure as a season-matched limit sized to the contract value, with receivables routed through us where possible. Take monthly: offtaker payment status, seed-lot inventory statement, and field-stage confirmation.

## Early-warning signs
- Offtaker payment delay beyond contract date (monthly) -> stop fresh disbursal and inspect the receivable.
- Inventory ageing past one sowing season (monthly) -> ask for the buyer's rejection or return record.
- Rainfall and sowing acreage in Jalna (weekly in season) -> if sowing falls, cut the next season's limit.
- Limit utilisation near the sanctioned cap (monthly) -> ask what the extra draw is funding before renewing.
